title: Scenario Planning with Agentic AI for Reinforcement Learning and Risk Mitigation in Developing Economies Business Education
venue: International Journal of Education, Business and Economics Research (IJEBER)
extended_summary:
The paper addresses the challenge of preparing business decision-makers in developing economies to operate under volatility, institutional voids, supply chain shocks, information asymmetry, and other sources of uncertainty. It argues that traditional case-based or lecture-based business education may not sufficiently develop adaptive decision-making, risk mitigation, and cognitive problem-solving skills for these contexts.

The intervention studied is the “Captains of Industry” simulation, an AI-augmented experiential learning platform for an Operations Management curriculum. The simulation uses agentic/generative AI to create bespoke business scenarios, update company data weekly, introduce shocks or “curveballs,” evaluate student decisions using rubrics, and provide qualitative feedback and performance scores. Students worked in management teams with roles such as CEO, CFO, procurement, information, and operations officers, making weekly decisions for simulated companies over a four-week period.

The study involved 125 university students working in simulated developing-economy business contexts, specifically framed around Latin America and the Caribbean. The authors used learning analytics and machine-learning methods, including Diffusion Maps and Kernel Two-Sample Tests, to analyze student performance trajectories, engagement, decision-making patterns, and differences between higher- and lower-performing students.

The paper concludes that the AI-augmented simulation supported reinforcement learning and helped develop decision-making and risk-mitigation capabilities, though outcomes varied substantially across students. The cohort achieved a mean score of 59.3%, with slightly more than half reaching a 60% proficiency threshold; 77 students improved, 32 declined, and 11 remained flat. Advanced analytics identified distinct micro-clusters and statistically separable achievement profiles, suggesting that the simulation can reveal different learning trajectories and support more targeted educational interventions.

identified_tools.name: Captains of Industry
identified_tools.description: An AI-assisted scenario-planning business simulation that generates dynamic company scenarios and provides rubric-aligned AI feedback and scores for experiential learning in operations management.
identified_tools.use_case: Used in an Operations Management curriculum with 125 university students to simulate developing-economy business contexts, generate bespoke scenarios and weekly business data, grade team decisions with AI against a rubric, and provide feedback for reinforcement learning and risk-mitigation practice.

findings.finding_summary: Among 125 university students using the Captains of Industry simulation, the cohort mean overall score, mean individual score, and mean group score were all 59.3%. A total of 51.2% of students achieved a score of 60% or higher, while the authors note that a substantial minority may require targeted support.
findings.measure: Overall, individual, and group simulation performance scores; percentage scoring 60% or higher

findings.finding_summary: The mean growth rate across the cohort was approximately 4.7% to 4.8%. Individual trajectories were heterogeneous: 77 students improved, 32 declined, and 11 remained flat; the highest reported individual growth was 43.6% and the lowest was -18.2%.
findings.measure: Growth rate learning trajectories in simulation performance

findings.finding_summary: Diffusion Maps identified non-linear geometric patterns and micro-clusters in the student feature space. A Kernel Two-Sample Test comparing top and bottom quartiles of overall performers found significantly different feature distributions, with Mean Maximum Discrepancy=0.722 and approximate p-value=0.012, which the authors interpret as separable achievement profiles.
findings.measure: Feature distributions of top and bottom quartiles of overall performers using Diffusion Maps and Kernel Two-Sample Test

findings.finding_summary: The mean take rate was 63.3%, indicating that students engaged with a substantial portion of available decision opportunities or activities in the simulation. The paper describes this as a significant level of engagement, while noting room to deepen participation.
findings.measure: Take rate / participation in simulation decision opportunities

quality_tier_rationale: The paper uses a design-based/pedagogical intervention approach with cohort analytics for 125 students, but it is not an RCT or QED and lacks a comparison group. Evidence is therefore observational/mixed-methods rather than causal.
impact_tier_rationale: Impact is positive but unclear: the study reports mean growth of 4.7%–4.8% and heterogeneous individual trajectories, but no control group, standardized effect size, or causal counterfactual is reported.
